common_name: Sweet Caroline Raven Sweet Potato Vine (Glossy Near-Black Fleur-de-Lis Leaf Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Raven was bred within the Sweet Caroline series for improved vigor and branching over older near-black selections like Blackie.

directions: Sweet Caroline Raven carries glossy, deeply lobed leaves shaped like small fleurs-de-lis in a rich purple-black that reads nearly jet black from a distance, giving it more sheen and a tighter, more mounded habit than the older ornamental sweet potato vine Blackie. It trails and cascades well over container edges and retaining walls while branching more freely than earlier near-black cultivars, which keeps the planting fuller without constant pinching. Grow it in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it is heat-tolerant and vigorous through the hottest part of summer, needing only occasional trimming to stay in scale within a mixed container or bed.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Sweetheart Lime Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Heart-Leaf Chartreuse Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Sweetheart Lime pairs the series' compact habit with distinctly heart-shaped, unlobed foliage rather than the ivy-like leaf of most sweet potato vine cultivars.

directions: Sweet Caroline Sweetheart Lime holds solid chartreuse, heart-shaped leaves that stay bright lime green through the season rather than fading to green the way some older chartreuse sweet potato vines do in heavy heat, and it greens up further when grown in light shade. Its restrained, well-mounded habit makes it easier to proportion in a mixed container than older, more rambunctious lime-foliage selections, while still trailing nicely over pot edges. Give it well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; like other Sweet Caroline types it tolerates heat well and needs only light trimming to keep it in bounds through summer.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Medusa Green Sweet Potato Vine (Multi-Fingered Sculptural Leaf Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Medusa Green's crown-shaped, multi-fingered leaves give a sculptural texture distinct from the broader-leaved Sweet Caroline and Illusion selections.

directions: Sweet Caroline Medusa Green stands apart from most ornamental sweet potato vines with narrow, radiating, multi-fingered leaves that give the plant a distinctly spiky, crown-like texture rather than the ivy-shaped foliage typical of the genus. It holds its fresh bright green color and vigorous growth through the hottest part of summer, forming a dense, textural mound that trails well over container edges and retaining walls. Grow it in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it is heat-tolerant and needs only occasional trimming, making a striking textural contrast when combined with broad-leaved or dark-foliage companions.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Medusa Black Sweet Potato Vine (Deeply Lobed Near-Black Lacy Leaf Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Medusa Black forms a dense, neat, mounded cloud of deeply lobed near-black leaves rather than sprawling the way older near-black cultivars do.

directions: Sweet Caroline Medusa Black bears deeply lobed, palm-shaped leaves so dark they appear nearly midnight black, layered into overlapping tiers that create a dense, billowy texture closer to a fern than to a typical trailing sweet potato vine. Its neat, self-contained mounded habit keeps the planting tidy without the regular trimming that rangier near-black cultivars often need. Grow it in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the deep color and fine-cut texture make it a strong contrast plant next to chartreuse or variegated foliage in containers, hanging baskets, and landscape beds.

common_name: Split Second Morning Glory (Frilled Double Bicolor Purple-and-Pink Vine)

planting.note: Nick or soak seeds overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow after last frost along a trellis or fence; morning glories resent transplanting.

directions: Nick the seed coat with a file or soak overnight, then direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a trellis or fence. Split Second is an heirloom morning glory grown for fully double, ruffled flowers with notched and frilled petal margins that give the bloom a peony- or parrot-tulip-like look rather than the familiar flat trumpet shape, colored a bicolor purple with a soft pink throat. Like other Ipomoea purpurea types it climbs vigorously by twining, opening fresh flowers each morning on new growth throughout the season. Deadhead spent flowers before seed set in warm climates to curb volunteer seedlings the following year.

common_name: Venice Blue Morning Glory (Heirloom Ultramarine-Striped White Trumpet Vine)

planting.note: Nick or soak seeds overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow after last frost along a trellis or fence; morning glories resent transplanting.

directions: Nick the seed coat with a file or soak overnight, then direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a trellis or fence. Venice Blue is an old heirloom morning glory bearing trumpet flowers of crisp white boldly striped with deep ultramarine blue, a distinctive picotee-edged pattern that has been illustrated in botanical publications for roughly two centuries. The vigorous twining vines climb quickly to cover a fence, arbor, or mailbox post in a single season, opening a fresh flush of striped blooms each morning. Deadhead spent flowers before seed set in warm climates, since Ipomoea purpurea self-sows readily where the season is long enough to mature seed.

common_name: Kikyo-zaki Morning Glory (Star-Shaped Semi-Double Japanese Morning Glory Mix)

planting.note: Nick or soak seeds overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow after last frost along a trellis, fence, or arbor; morning glories resent transplanting.

directions: Nick the seed coat with a file or soak overnight, then direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a trellis or fence. Kikyo-zaki is a traditional Japanese Asagao strain of Ipomoea nil grown for star-shaped, often semi-double flowers with a crisp white picotee edge, blooming in a mix of red, white, and blue across the planting. The vigorous climbing vines reach 8 to 10 feet in a single season, opening a fresh crop of star-form flowers each dawn through summer and into fall. Deadhead spent blooms before seed set where volunteer seedlings are not wanted the following year.

common_name: Kanoko Red Speckled Morning Glory (Pink-Speckled White Japanese Morning Glory with Variegated Leaves)

planting.note: Nick or soak seeds overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow after last frost along a trellis or fence; morning glories resent transplanting.

directions: Nick the seed coat with a file or soak overnight, then direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a trellis or fence. Kanoko Red Speckled is a striking Japanese morning glory with snow-white, medium-sized flowers speckled and streaked in flamingo pink, carried on vigorous vines that also display handsome variegated foliage, a double point of interest unusual among morning glories. Plants climb 8 to 12 feet in a season, opening fresh speckled blooms each morning through summer and fall. Deadhead spent flowers before seed set in long-season climates to limit volunteer seedlings.
